column2: He who saw the wellspring, the ground-course of the land,
[who knew the way]s, was wise in everything —
[Gilgameš, who] saw the wellspring, the ground-course of the land,
[who knew the way]s, was wise in everything.
He surveyed the shrines everywhere alike;
he knew the sum of the wisdom of all things.
He saw the guarded thing, uncovered the covered,
brought back word of the time before the Flood.
He walked the long road, worn out, and was stilled.
He fixed on a stone stela the whole of his labor.
He built up the rampart of Uruk-the-Sheepfold,
of hallowed Eanna, the shining storehouse.
Look at its wall, its coping like carded wool;
study its parapet, which no one can copy.
Take the stair that has stood from the first days;
go close to Eanna, the dwelling of Ištar,
which no later king — no one at all — can copy.
Go up on the wall of Uruk; walk its circuit.
Test the platform; consider the brickwork:
is its brick not brick fired in a kiln?
Did the Seven Counsellors not lay down its footing?
[A šār] of city, a šār of orchard, a šār of clay-pit, the open ground of Ištar's house:
three šār and the open ground — the survey of Uruk.
[Open] the tablet-box of cedar;
[undo] its clasps of bronze;
[open] the door on its guarded thing;
[lift] out the tablet of lapis lazuli and read aloud
[everyth]ing Gilgameš went through, all the hardship.
[Surp]assing all kings, celebrated, lordly of stature,
[he]ro born of Uruk, wild bull always butting:
he goes in front, the foremost,
and he goes behind, the trust of his brothers —
a strong bank, the shelter of his troops,
a furious flood-wave that wrecks a wall of stone.
Wild bull of Lugalbanda, Gilgameš, perfect in strength,
suckling of the august cow, of Wild-Cow Ninsun:
towering Gilgameš, perfect, dread-inspiring,
opener of passes through the mountain-ranges,
digger of wells on the mountains' flank,
crosser of the ocean, the wide sea, as far as sunrise,
scanner of the world's rims, forever hunting life,
who reached by main strength Ūta-napišti the Far-away,
restorer of cult-towns that the Flood destroyed,
establisher of rites for the teeming peoples.
Who is there to rival him in kingship
and say, like Gilgameš, "It is I who am king"?
Gilgameš was his name from the day of his birth,
two-thirds of him god and one-third of him human.
The Lady-of-the-Gods drew the form of his body;
Nudimmud brought his figure to perfection.
[ ... ] majestic of stature [ ... ]
[ ... ] eleven cubits [was his height,]
[four cubits] the span [of his chest;]
a triple cubit his foot, half a rod his stride,
six cubits the reach of [his legs,]
[three cu]bits the forelock of his cheek;
his cheeks were bearded like [lapis lazuli,]
the locks of his hair sprou[ting rank as barley.]
Grown to his full height, perfect in his splen[dor,]
by earthly reckoning he was made most fair.
In the Sheepfold of Uruk he goes st[riding];
he lords it like a wild bull, head carried high.
He has no rival when his weapons are raised;
at the ball-game his companions are kept on their feet.
The young men of Uruk he harries without cause,
and Gilgameš lets no son go free to his fa[ther;]
[da]y and [nig]ht he storms with growing fury —
[Gilgā]meš, k[ing of the teeming peoples,]
he, the shep[herd] of Uruk-the-Sheep[fold] —
and Gilgameš lets no [daughter go free to] her mother.
[He is their wild bull;] they are the cows.
Their com[plaint went up ... ]
Mighty one, [splendid, expert ... ]
Gilgameš lets [no] girl go free t[o her bridegroom,]
the warrior's daughter, the young man's br[ide.]
Their complaint Iš[tar] he[ard again and again;]
[the god]s of heaven, the lords of comm[and:]

You made rear up in Uruk-the-Sheepfold a battering wild bull:

84	day and nig[ht he storms] with growing fury —
85	he, the shepherd of Uruk-the-Sheepfold,
86	Gilgameš, [the herdsman of the teeming peo]ples —
87	he is their shepherd, and yet [ ... them;]
88	[m]ighty, splendid, expert [ ... ]
89	Gilgameš lets no girl go free to her b[ridegroom,]
90	the warrior's daughter, the young man's bri[de.]
Their complaint [Anu] heard again and again.
They cried out to Aruru, the great one:

You, Aruru, made mankind;
94	now build the double of him —
95	to the storm of his heart let it be equal.
96	Let them contend with each other, and Uruk find q[uiet.]
When Aruru heard this,
she built inside her the double that Anu spoke.
Aruru washed her hands,
pinched off clay, cast it down in the open land.
In the open land she built Enkidu, a fighting man,
offspring of stillness, knotted hard by Ninurta.
All his body is shaggy with hair,
his head of hair grown out like a woman's,
its locks sprouting rank as barley.
He knows no people, no land at all;
he goes dressed like Šakkan.
With the gazelles he eats grass;
with the herd he crowds in at the watering-place;
with the beasts of the steppe his heart is glad at the water.
A hunter, a man who sets snares,
came up against him at the lip of the watering-place —
one day, a second, a third, at the lip of the watering-place.
The hunter saw him, and his face went dead-still.
He and his herd — it went back into its lair,
while he, [tro]ubled, fell dumb, fell still;
his heart [ ... ], his face went dark,
misery lodged in his belly,
his face like one come off a long road.
The hunter shaped [his mouth] to speak, saying [to his father:]

Father, there is a young man who ca[me here] —
122	in [all the land] his strength [is] the strongest;
123	his might is as hard [as a lump] of the sky-rock of Anu.
124	[He roa]ms over the hills all [the time;]
125	all the time with the herd [I see him] grazing;
126	all the time his [fe]et [are planted] at the lip of the watering-place.
127	[I am afraid; I dare no]t go near h[im.]
128	[He fills in the pi]ts I myself dig;
129	[he tears out the] traps I sp[read;]
130	[he frees from my hands] the herds, the beasts of the ste[ppe;]
131	he will not let me work the steppe.
[His father shaped his mouth to spe]ak, saying to the hunter:
["Go, my son. Inside] Uruk [lives] Gilgameš:
[ ... ] over him;
his might is as hard [as a lump of the sky-rock of Anu.]
[Take the road; toward Uruk se]t your face.
[ ... ] the strength of a man.
[Go, my son, and lead back with you the harlot Šamhat;]
[ ... ] like a strong one.
[When the herd comes do]wn [to] the watering-place,
[let her strip off her clo]thing [and lay bare her al]lure:
he will [se]e her, and he will come clo[se to her,]
and his herd will turn stranger to him, [though it grew up on] his steppe."
Heeding the counsel of his father, [ ... ]
the hunter went off [ ... ];
he took the road, inside Uruk he s[et his face,]
and to the kin[g, Gil]ga[meš, he rep]eated his report:
Gilgameš said to him, to the hunter:

Go, hunter; lead back with you the harlot Šamhat.
161	When the herd co[mes dow]n to the watering-place,
162	let her strip off [her] clothing [and lay ba]re her allure:
163	he will see her, and he will come close to her,
164	and his herd will turn stranger to him, th[ough it g]rew up on his steppe.
The hunter went; he led with him the harlot Šamhat.
They took the road, they set straight on the way;
on the third day they arrived at the appointed field.
Hunter and harlot sat down at their posts:
one day, a second day, they sat at the lip of the watering-place.
The herd came down; it was drinking at the watering-place;
the beasts arrived, their hearts glad at the water —
and he too, Enkidu, whose birthplace was the hills:
with the gazelles he eats grass;
with the herd he crowds in at the watering-place;
with the beasts of the steppe his heart is glad at the water.
Šamhat saw him — the first-made man,
the murderous young male from the middle of the steppe.

There he is, Šamhat! Loosen the fold of your arms;
179	open your lap; let him take your allure.
180	Do not hold back; take his breath from him.
181	He will see you, and he will come close to you.
182	Spread out your clothing; let him lie on you;
183	work on the man the work of a woman.
184	His herd will turn stranger to him, though it grew up on his steppe,
185	while his lovemaking murmurs over you.
Šamhat let loose her skirts;
she opened her lap, and he took her allure.
She did not hold back; she took his breath from him.
She spread out her clothing, and he lay on her;
she worked on the man, the first-made man, the work of a woman,
while his lovemaking murmured over her.
Six days and seven nights Enkidu, aroused, poured himself into Šamhat.
When he was sated with her delights
he set his face toward his herd —
and seeing him, Enkidu, the gazelles bolted;
the beasts of the steppe shrank from his body.
Enkidu had spent himself; his body was scoured clean;
his knees stood locked while his herd went away.
Enkidu was lessened; his running was not as before —
and he: he had ear now, and a widened understanding.
He turned back and sat down at the harlot's feet,
watching the harlot's face,
and what the harlot said, his ears were hearing.
[The harlot] said to him, to Enkidu:

You are [fai]r, Enkidu; you are become like a god.
206	Why rove the open land with the beasts?
207	Come, let me lead you into Uruk-the-Sheepfold,
208	to the holy house, the seat of Anu and Ištar,
208a	[Come, let me lead you] into Uruk-the-Sheepfold,
208b	[to the] hallowed [Eanna], the seat of Ištar,
209	where Gilgameš is, perfect in strength,
210	and lords it like a wild bull over the young men.
She was speaking to him, and her speech found favor:
knowing his own heart now, he was looking for a friend.
Enkidu said to her, to the harlot:

Come, Šamhat; take me along,
215	to the holy house, the hallowed seat of Anu and Ištar,
216	where Gilgameš is, perfect in strength,
217	and lords it like a wild bull over the young men.
218	I will challenge him — strong is [ ... ] —
219	[I will bo]ast in the middle of Uruk: 'It is I who am mighty!'
220	[ ... ] I will change the order of things —
221	[the one bo]rn in the open land is strongest of all!

[Let the people] see your face —
223	[ ... ] that there is; I know it well.
224	G[o,] Enkidu, t[o Uru]k-the-Sheepfold,
225	wh[ere the young m]en are girded with sashes,
226	where ev[ery da]y [ ... ] a festival is held,
227	whe[re] the drums [are ratt]ling out,
228	and the g[ir]ls are shapely of figure,
229	adorned with allure, [fu]ll of gladness;
230	on the couch of night the great ones are brought out.
231	Enkid[u — you who know no]thing of living —
232	I will show you Gilgameš, a man glad-and-grieving.
233	Look at him; gaze on his face:
234	he is beautiful in manhood, carries dignity,
235	his whole body adorned with allure.
236	He has strength mightier than yours;
237	he is one who does not sleep day or night.
238	Enkidu, put away your sin of pride:
239	Gilgameš — Šamaš loves him;
240	Anu, Enlil, and Ea widened his understanding.
241	Before you ever came down from the hills,
242	Gilgameš inside Uruk was seeing you in dreams.
Gilgameš rose to unravel a dream, saying to his mother:

Mother, this is the dream I saw in my night:
245	the stars of the sky came out for me,
246	and like a lump of the sky-rock of Anu one kept falling down at me.
247	I lifted it: it was too strong for me;
248	I heaved at it: I could not shift it.
249	The land of Uruk was standing over it,
250	[the land gathered] about it,
251	[the crow]d [pressing] i[n up]on i[t,]
252	[the young men hea]ped up around it;
253	[like a nursli]ng infant they kissed [its] feet.
254	[I loved it li]ke a wife: I bent murmuring over it,
255	[I lifted it and s]et it down at [your] feet,
256	[and you — you ma]de it equal with m[e.]
[The mother of Gilgam]eš, clever, expert, all-knowing, said to her son —
[Wild-Cow Ninsun,] clever, expert, all-knowing, said to Gilgameš:
He saw a second dream.
He rose and went in before the goddess his mother;
Gilgameš said to her, to his mother:

Once more, mother, I have seen a dream:
275	[in the street] of Uruk-of-the-Squares
276	an axe was lying, and around it they gathered;
277	the land of [Uru]k was standing over it,
278	[the land gath]ered about it,
279	the crowd pressing in upon it.
280	[The young men hea]ped up around it.
281	I lifted it and set it down at your feet;
282	[I love]d it like a wife, bending murmuring over it,
283	[and yo]u — you made it equal with me.
The mother of Gilgameš, clever, expert, all-knowing, said to her son —
[Wild-Cow Ninsun,] clever, expert, all-knowing, said to Gilgameš:

My son, the axe you saw is a man.
287	You will love him like a wife, bending murmuring over him,
288	and I — I will make him equal with you:
289	there will come to you a strong one, a companion, the rescuer of a friend.
290	In all the land his strength is the strongest;
291	his might is as hard as a lump of the sky-rock of Anu.
Gilgameš said to her, to his mother:
[So he s]aw his dreams —
[and after] Šamhat had told Gilgameš's dreams to Enkidu,
the two of them [fell to lo]ving one another.
